title: Supreme Court gives Centre and Delhi 10 days to answer pleas over anti-CEC protest detentions
dek: Petitioners say thousands were held during the October protests against the Chief Election Commissioner. Delhi Police says no one was arrested or detained.
body:
The Supreme Court on Wednesday ordered the Centre and the Delhi government to file comprehensive replies within 10 days to a batch of petitions alleging illegal detentions of political leaders, protesters and lawyers during the October protests in Delhi against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Petitioners may file their responses within a further week.

The bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana acted after Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati told it that the government's affidavits had been filed in only some of the petitions, according to reports of the hearing. The court said it would take the matter up again after the replies are in. No date for the next hearing was reported.

## The competing accounts

The lead petition is a habeas corpus plea filed by Menaka Guruswamy, a senior advocate and Trinamool Congress member of the Rajya Sabha. It concerns the alleged removal of Mamata Banerjee, the former chief minister of West Bengal and the Trinamool leader, from the protest site, and the detention of other political leaders.

Delhi Police has told the court that Ms Guruswamy's petition has become infructuous because nobody was arrested or detained during the 10 October protest. When the Chief Justice asked on Wednesday whether anyone was still in detention, Ms Bhati said no one had been detained even when the plea was filed, reports said.

The petitioners' account is very different. According to reports, more than 7,000 people were detained over the two days of protests, including Abhijit Dipke of the Cockroach Janta Party, several opposition leaders and the YouTuber Dhruv Rathee. That figure comes from the petitioners and from reports at the time; it has not been confirmed by the police or the court.

## What else is before the court

The batch includes a plea by AA Rahim, a Rajya Sabha member of the CPI(M), and petitions by the Supreme Court Bar Association and the Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association over police action against lawyers who joined the protests. Other petitions challenge the closure of metro stations and disruption of trains before the protests, allege assaults on protesters and on women journalists covering them, and seek contempt action against Union Home Secretary Govind Mohan, Delhi Police Commissioner Anurag Kumar and the Delhi Metro's chief, D Thara, for allegedly disobeying an order to lift the transport restrictions.

At a special sitting on 11 October, the court observed that people in peaceful gatherings should not face illegal detention and asked the Centre to keep the Delhi Metro running normally and to avoid internet shutdowns, subject to law-and-order needs.

## Background

The protests on 10 and 11 October were called by opposition parties and civil-society groups demanding Mr Kumar's removal over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, which has deleted large numbers of names in several states, including West Bengal.

On 3 November the same bench, while organising the many connected cases into nine categories for hearing, said that no single group could occupy a designated protest site indefinitely. Delhi's traders' associations have separately asked the court to restrict protests, saying they lost business during the festive season.

## What happens next

The Centre and the Delhi government now have until early December to put their full account of what happened on 10 and 11 October on record. The court is then expected to hear the detention petitions alongside the other categories of the protest cases.

This story is based on reports of the hearing; the court's written order had not been published by Wednesday evening.
